fieldNotes.title: Field Notes: The 4.7% Endowment vs the 11.8% Index
fieldNotes.source: Practising CA in Pune, partner at a fictional firm Bhide & Sathe Associates, after a Diwali family lunch with a school friend
fieldNotes.story:
At Diwali 2024 my friend — call him Ravi, 38, mid-level IT manager — proudly showed me a maturity statement from an LIC endowment policy his father had bought him in **2002**.

Premium: **₹24,000/year** for 21 years. Total paid in: **₹5.04L**. Maturity (with 'bonuses'): **₹13.6L** in 2023.

Ravi was beaming. *'See, more than 2.5x.'*

I asked if I could open a calculator. The IRR worked out to **4.7%** — actually below CPI inflation over the same period (~5.4%). In real terms, **he had lost purchasing power**.

Then I ran the alternative. The same **₹24K/year** invested annually in a Nifty 50 index fund from 2002 to 2023 (XIRR via Value Research, dividend reinvested):

- Total invested: **₹5.04L** (identical)
- Terminal value: **₹52.8L**
- Effective IRR: **~13.1%**
- Gap vs the LIC endowment: **₹39.2L of foregone wealth**

The punchline: **Ravi's father did not save him ₹39.2L of risk. He spent ₹39.2L of compounding to buy an emotional sense of safety**, sold to him by an LIC agent in 2002 who was paid a 35% first-year commission.

Ravi was quiet for the rest of the lunch. The samosas got cold.
fieldNotes.takeaway: The cost of a 'safe' investment is not the lower return — it is the trillion small compounding events you didn't get. Compounding doesn't punish risk-aversion in year 1. It punishes it in year 21.

bossBattle.title: Aarav vs the ULIP
bossBattle.setup:
Aarav, 31, calls in a panic between meetings. Cleaning out a cupboard at his mother's place in Pune, he found a **ULIP policy** she bought him in **2019** as a 'wedding gift advance'. He never paid attention to it. SBI Life Smart Wealth Builder, premium **₹60,000/year**, locked for 5 years.

The numbers as of today:

- Years paid: **5 of 5** (lock-in just ended last month)
- Total premium paid: **₹3.0L**
- Current fund value: **₹3.42L**
- Effective IRR: **~3.8%**
- Surrender value if he exits today: **₹3.42L** (no surrender charge post lock-in)
- Continue option: pay ₹60K/year for 10 more years, projected maturity ~₹14L at the policy's 'illustrated' 8% (which the IRDAI documents disclose may not materialise)

His mother is on the call. She is upset that he is even *considering* surrendering. *'Beta, agent-uncle said this is the safest one. Why are you listening to some YouTube person?'*

Your move.

coach.name: FIRE-walla Falguni
coach.role: Ex-Deutsche Bank, retired at 41, runs a personal-finance Substack from Goa

stages.prompt:
First question — should Aarav surrender today, continue paying, or convert to paid-up?

Assume he can redirect the **₹60K/year** premium into a Nifty 50 index fund instead.

options.label: Continue paying. Insurance-cum-investment is balanced; surrendering 'wastes' the 5 years.
options.explain: **Sunk cost fallacy in pure form.** The ₹3L is gone whether he stays or leaves. The only question is what the *next* ₹6L (10 × ₹60K) earns. At the policy's 3.8% IRR vs the index's long-term ~12%, continuing for 10 more years costs roughly **₹4.8L in foregone wealth** — to keep a sub-inflation product alive.

options.label: Surrender now. Take the ₹3.42L, redirect the future ₹60K/year to a Nifty 50 index fund.
options.explain: Correct. Lock-in is over, no surrender charge, and the *forward* expected value of the ₹3.42L + ₹60K/year flowing into an index fund vastly outperforms continuing the ULIP. Re-running the field-notes maths: ₹3.42L lump + ₹60K/year for 10 years at 12% ≈ **₹21.5L**. ULIP same horizon at 8% illustrated ≈ ~₹14L. Difference of **~₹7.5L for one decision today**.

options.label: Convert to paid-up: stop paying, let the existing ₹3L grow inside the policy. Best of both worlds.
options.explain: Paid-up status freezes the corpus inside the same low-return ULIP — it keeps eating mortality charges and fund management fees but you've stopped feeding it. You get the worst of both: capital trapped at 3.8% AND no new compounding. Surrender beats paid-up here because the fund value is already above premium paid.

options.label: Surrender, but keep the ₹3.42L in a 5-year FD 'because it was meant for the wedding'.
options.explain: Right call on surrender, wrong call on redeployment. FD at 7% pre-tax = ~5% post-tax for Aarav's bracket = barely above inflation. He just escaped one sub-inflation trap; don't park the proceeds in another. Index fund or, if the wedding really is 12 months away, a debt fund — not an FD with an emotional tag.

stages.prompt:
Aarav's mother is now actively crying. *'But the agent said this gives life cover too! If something happens to you, this protects Meera.'*

How do you handle the emotional + technical layer at once?

options.label: Soften: keep paying for the 'life cover peace of mind', it's not a huge amount.
options.explain: Avoiding the conversation costs Aarav real money. The ULIP's life cover is **₹6L** — laughably inadequate for an engaged 31-year-old engineer. Real life cover for him should be **₹2-3 crore term insurance** at roughly **₹14-18K/year**. The ULIP is the wrong product for both jobs it claims to do.

options.label: Decouple insurance and investment cleanly: buy a ₹2 crore term plan (~₹15K/year), surrender the ULIP, invest the rest in an index. Tell mom: 'Meera is more protected, not less.'
options.explain: This is the script. The ULIP fails at *both* jobs — the cover is inadequate AND the returns are sub-inflation. Term + index gives mom what she actually wants (Meera protected) at a fraction of the cost, AND wealth that compounds. Frame it as upgrading her gift, not rejecting it.

options.label: Show mom the IRR spreadsheet. Numbers don't lie.
options.explain: Numbers don't lie, but they also don't persuade your mother. The agent sold her *trust*, not maths. Counter with story (Ravi's ₹39L gap from the field notes), then with a better gift (term + index in *her* name as the gift-giver). Spreadsheets lose to feelings; better stories beat both.

stages.prompt:
Plan accepted. Aarav surrenders the ULIP, buys term insurance, redirects to index. He asks: *'Falguni — assume I do this religiously, ₹60K/year into the Nifty for the next 30 years until I'm 61. What does compounding actually look like for *that* one decision?'*

Pick the most useful answer:

options.label: ₹60K × 30 years = ₹18L invested. At 12% it's about ₹1.45 crore. Decent.
options.explain: Maths is right, narration is wrong. 'Decent' undersells the compounding cascade. Of that ₹1.45 crore, only **₹18L (12%) is your money** — the other **₹1.27 crore (88%) is compounding doing the work.** That ratio is the single most important fact in personal finance and Aarav should feel it in his bones.

options.label: ₹1.45 crore at age 61 — but the magic isn't the number. **The last 10 years of that 30 generate ₹86L of the ₹1.45 cr.** Compounding is back-loaded; that's why surrendering the ULIP today (year 0) matters so much more than a similar fix at year 20.
options.explain: This is *the* answer. The compounding cascade is non-linear — it whispers for 15 years and roars for the last 10. Every year of delay isn't 'one year' of cost, it's one year *off the loud end*. That's why a 31-year-old surrendering a bad product today saves more than a 41-year-old surrendering the same product, even though the 41-year-old has paid more in.

options.label: Don't promise 12% — that's optimistic. Use 8% and say ₹73L.
options.explain: Conservatism is good but the wrong frame here. The Nifty 50 has delivered **~12.4% CAGR over the last 25 years** including 2008 and 2020. Quoting 8% to be 'safe' makes the index look only marginally better than the ULIP and undercuts the whole intervention. Use rolling-period averages, name the assumption, then own the number.

outcomes.perfect: You just saved Aarav approximately ₹7.5L in foregone wealth from this single decision, set him up for ₹1+ crore of additional terminal wealth at 61, AND defused the family-WhatsApp battle by upgrading his mother's gift instead of rejecting it. This is what good advice actually looks like.
outcomes.good: Right call on surrender, slightly soft on the term insurance or the redeployment vehicle. Aarav is meaningfully better off but might leave ₹2-3L on the table over 30 years.
outcomes.learn: The ULIP is still in force. Mom is happy. In 2055 Aarav will be Ravi from the field notes, looking at a maturity statement with a 5% IRR and the ₹39L hole where compounding should have been. Re-read the field notes. The cost is paid in year 21, not year 1.
